title: Noisy-Pair Robust Representation Alignment for Positive-Unlabeled Learning
claim: Representation learning pulls same-class pairs from different supervision sources; ours stays robust when those pairs come from unreliable labels.
layout: 3 panels, left-to-right, dashed circle embedding space with image samples
description: Three side-by-side panels separated by vertical lines. Each shows a gradient gray dashed circle as the embedding space. An anchor photo of a dog sits at upper left, and a same-class sample sits at lower left. Different-class samples, a white cat and a white running dog, sit at upper right. Black lines link same-class images to the circle, and red lines link different-class images. Panel (a) is self-supervised: the same-class sample is an augmented anchor, and the other images have green and yellow borders. Panel (b) is supervised: a blue dashed box groups clean same-class samples, and a pink dashed box groups different-class samples. Panel (c) is noisy-pair robust: the labels are corrupted, so a white dog is wrongly treated as different-class and a cat is wrongly placed among same-class samples. Italic captions in boxes name the pair source. Bold panel titles sit at the bottom.
caption: Illustration of different representation learning methods. Representation learning can acquire discriminative representations either by pulling same-class samples closer to the anchor and pushing different-class samples apart (contrastive representation learning), or by only pulling same-class samples closer to the anchor (non-contrastive representation learning). (a) Self-supervised representation learning: same-class pairs from augmented anchor. (b) Supervised representation learning: same-class pairs from reliable labels. (c) Noisy-pair robust representation learning: same-class pairs from unreliable labels.
abstract: Positive-Unlabeled (PU) learning aims to train a binary classifier (positive vs. negative) where only limited positive data and abundant unlabeled data are available. While widely applicable, state-of-the-art PU learning methods substantially underperform their supervised counterparts on complex datasets, especially without auxiliary negatives or pre-estimated parameters (e.g., a 14.26% gap on CIFAR-100 dataset). We identify the primary bottleneck as the challenge of learning discriminative representations under unreliable supervision. To tackle this challenge, we propose NcPU, a non-contrastive PU learning framework that requires no auxiliary information. NcPU combines a noisy-pair robust supervised non-contrastive loss (NoiSNCL), which aligns intra-class representations despite unreliable supervision, with a phantom label disambiguation (PLD) scheme that supplies conservative negative supervision via regret-based label updates. Theoretically, NoiSNCL and PLD can iteratively benefit each other from the perspective of the Expectation-Maximization framework. Empirically, extensive experiments demonstrate that: (1) NoiSNCL enables simple PU methods to achieve competitive performance; and (2) NcPU achieves substantial improvements over state-of-the-art PU methods across diverse datasets, including challenging datasets on post-disaster building damage mapping, highlighting its promise for real-world applications.
